did_you_know.text: Did you know? Micah opens with the image of someone looking for fruit after summer and the grape harvest, but finding not even a single cluster. This image expresses the sense that good people and worthy deeds are in short supply.

Did you know? This verse states explicitly: “The godly have perished from the land; there is no upright person among the people.” The prophet describes a society in which violence and persecution damage relationships between people as well.
Did you know? Micah describes a corrupt government and legal system: the official demands a bribe, the judge rules in exchange for payment, and the powerful use their influence to get what they want.
Did you know? The corruption in the chapter is so deep that the prophet warns against trusting even a friend or one’s closest companion. This is a description of a broad social crisis of trust.

Did you know? The breakdown of society reaches into the family as well: a son dishonors his father, a daughter rises against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Therefore, a person’s enemies are the members of his own household.
Did you know? After describing the corrupt society, the prophet adopts a personal stance of faith: he looks to the LORD, waits for the God of his salvation, and trusts that the LORD will hear him.
Did you know? The phrase “Though I have fallen, I will rise” expresses the hope that one can get back up after falling. Even when Israel sits in darkness, the LORD is described as its light.

Did you know? The prophet does not ignore sin: he is willing to bear the LORD’s anger until the LORD carries out his judgment and brings him into the light. In this way, the chapter combines acknowledgment of guilt with trust in the LORD’s justice.

Did you know? Micah asks the LORD to shepherd his people like a flock and restore them to the pastures of Bashan and Gilead. The request portrays Israel as “the flock of your inheritance,” under the care of its shepherd.

Did you know? The request to restore Israel also includes the renewal of wonders like those performed during the exodus from Egypt. Thus, the exodus serves in this chapter as a model for a future act of salvation.
Did you know? The chapter’s conclusion emphasizes the LORD’s character: he pardons iniquity, overlooks transgression, and does not remain angry forever, because he delights in mercy.

Did you know? The conclusion of the book of Micah connects the LORD’s forgiveness with his faithfulness to the covenant: “faithfulness to Jacob” and “steadfast love to Abraham” are given in accordance with the promises sworn to the ancestors long ago.
